courses.subject: ELA
courses.title: English 12 – World & British Literature + Senior Research
courses.description: A senior English course that traces British and world literature from Beowulf and Chaucer through Shakespeare, the Romantics, the Victorians, colonial and postcolonial voices, and Modernism. Students write the UC Personal Insight Questions and college essays in the fall, produce literary analyses and a timed-writing portfolio, and complete a six-week Senior Research Paper (MLA) with an oral defense. Grammar, vocabulary, and speaking & listening are woven into every week.
courses.framework: California Common Core State Standards for ELA/Literacy (grades 11–12); 2014 California ELA/ELD Framework

standards.RL.11-12.1: Cite strong, thorough textual evidence for explicit meaning and inferences, including where the text leaves matters uncertain.
standards.RL.11-12.2: Determine two or more themes and analyze their development and interaction; provide an objective summary.
standards.RL.11-12.3: Analyze the impact of an author's choices about developing and relating elements of a story or drama.
standards.RL.11-12.4: Determine meaning of words and phrases, including figurative and connotative language; analyze impact of word choice on tone, including multiple-meaning words and fresh, engaging language (Shakespeare and others).
standards.RL.11-12.5: Analyze how an author's choices concerning structure contribute to overall meaning and aesthetic impact.
standards.RL.11-12.6: Analyze a case where grasping point of view requires distinguishing what is directly stated from what is meant (satire, sarcasm, irony, understatement).
standards.RL.11-12.7: Analyze multiple interpretations of a story, drama, or poem (recorded or live production), evaluating how each interprets the source text.
standards.RL.11-12.9: Demonstrate knowledge of foundational works of literature, including how two or more texts from the same period treat similar themes or topics.
standards.RL.11-12.10: Read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, at the high end of the grades 11–CCR text complexity band independently.
standards.RI.11-12.1: Cite strong, thorough textual evidence to support analysis of informational text.
standards.RI.11-12.2: Determine two or more central ideas of a text and analyze their development; provide an objective summary.
standards.RI.11-12.3: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how individuals, ideas, or events interact.
standards.RI.11-12.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases in a text, including how an author refines the meaning of a key term over the course of a text.
standards.RI.11-12.5: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in an exposition or argument.
standards.RI.11-12.6: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective.
standards.RI.11-12.7: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats to address a question or solve a problem.
standards.RI.11-12.8: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal texts, including the premises, purposes, and arguments.
standards.RI.11-12.10: Read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 11–CCR text complexity band independently.
standards.W.11-12.1: Write arguments to support claims using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.
standards.W.11-12.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas clearly and accurately.
standards.W.11-12.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences using effective technique, well-chosen details, and well-structured event sequences.
standards.W.11-12.4: Produce clear and coherent writing appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
standards.W.11-12.5: Develop and strengthen writing by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.
standards.W.11-12.6: Use technology to produce, publish, and update individual or shared writing products in response to ongoing feedback.
standards.W.11-12.7: Conduct short and sustained research projects to answer a question or solve a problem; synthesize multiple sources.
standards.W.11-12.8: Gather relevant information from multiple authoritative print and digital sources; assess strengths and limitations of each; integrate information while avoiding plagiarism and following a standard citation format.
standards.W.11-12.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
standards.W.11-12.10: Write routinely over extended and shorter time frames for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.
standards.SL.11-12.1: Initiate and participate effectively in collaborative discussions, building on others' ideas and expressing one's own clearly and persuasively.
standards.SL.11-12.3: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.
standards.SL.11-12.4: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence conveying a clear and distinct perspective appropriate to purpose, audience, and task.
standards.SL.11-12.5: Make strategic use of digital media in presentations to enhance understanding of findings, reasoning, and evidence.
standards.SL.11-12.6: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when appropriate.
standards.L.11-12.1: Demonstrate command of standard English grammar and usage; apply the understanding that usage is a matter of convention that changes over time.
standards.L.11-12.2: Demonstrate command of standard English capitalization, punctuation (including hyphenation conventions), and spelling.
standards.L.11-12.3: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts and to make effective choices for meaning or style.
standards.L.11-12.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words using context, word parts, and reference materials.
standards.L.11-12.5: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
standards.L.11-12.6: Acquire and use accurately general academic and domain-specific words and phrases.

units.title: Voice & the College Essay

units.big_idea: Early English literature reveals what a culture honors, fears, and satirizes.

units.big_idea: Tragedy shows how unchecked ambition corrupts both a person and a kingdom.

objectives: Analyze how essayists use specific detail and reflection
Brainstorm a bank of personal stories

days.title: What makes a voice
days.work: Read Brian Doyle's short essay 'Joyas Voladoras' (or any short personal essay from the library) and annotate three moments where a concrete detail carries emotion. Write a paragraph on the essay's tone.

days.title: Life inventory
days.work: Complete a 'life inventory' brainstorm: 10 places, 10 people, 10 challenges, 10 things you do without being asked. Star the three stories with the most specific memories.

days.title: Show, then reflect
days.work: Study the narrative-to-reflection ratio by highlighting story sentences vs. insight sentences in a model essay. Freewrite 300 words on one starred story, ending with what it taught you.

days.title: Grammar: sentence variety
days.work: Mini-lesson on varying sentence openings (participial phrase, subordinate clause, prepositional phrase). Revise your freewrite so no two consecutive sentences begin the same way.

days.title: Read-aloud & check
days.work: Read your freewrite aloud to a parent and get two 'I want to know more about…' questions. Submit the freewrite with a 3-sentence self-reflection on voice.

weeks.assessment: Freewrite scored on specific detail and reflection; brainstorm inventory complete.

objectives: Match personal stories to UC PIQ prompts

days.title: Decoding the prompts
days.work: Read all eight UC Personal Insight Questions and the UC tips page. Chart which of your starred stories fits each prompt and choose your four.

days.title: Draft PIQ #1
days.work: Draft the first PIQ response (350-word limit) using a 'moment → action → result → meaning' structure.

days.title: Draft PIQ #2
days.work: Draft a second PIQ on a different prompt, making sure it reveals a different side of you than PIQ #1.

days.title: Concision workshop
days.work: Cut each draft by 15% by removing filler words (very, really, in order to), passive constructions, and repeated ideas. Track word counts before and after.

days.title: Peer-style review
days.work: Exchange drafts with a parent or mentor using a checklist (specific? answers the prompt? shows impact?). Write a revision plan for each response.

weeks.assessment: Two complete PIQ drafts under 350 words with a written revision plan.

objectives: Revise for clarity, specificity, and voice
Finalize four PIQs and a Common App-style essay outline

days.title: Draft PIQs #3–4
days.work: Draft the remaining two PIQ responses, choosing at least one that addresses academic interest or community contribution.

days.title: Cliché hunt
days.work: Mini-lesson on diction: replace every cliché and vague abstraction ('passionate,' 'made me who I am') with a concrete image or action in all four drafts.

days.title: Mechanics edit
days.work: Edit all four PIQs for comma splices, run-ons, and apostrophe errors using a mechanics checklist; read each aloud backwards sentence by sentence to catch typos.

days.title: Mock interview
days.work: Do a 10-minute mock admissions conversation with a parent, answering 'Tell me about yourself' and one question drawn from each PIQ.

days.title: Publish & reflect
days.work: Submit final versions of four PIQs (each ≤350 words) and write a one-paragraph reflection on your biggest revision change.

weeks.assessment: Final four PIQs scored with a college-essay rubric (specificity, insight, voice, conventions).

objectives: Identify features of epic poetry and the Anglo-Saxon heroic code
Analyze Beowulf's character through his boasts and deeds
materials: Beowulf (Gummere translation, Project Gutenberg, or Heaney translation from library)

days.title: Anglo-Saxon world
days.work: Read a short overview of Anglo-Saxon England and the Sutton Hoo ship burial; list five values a warrior culture would prize. Read 'The Seafarer' and mark where Christian and pagan ideas collide.

days.title: Grendel attacks
days.work: Read Beowulf lines 1–700 (Prologue through Beowulf's arrival). Collect 8 kennings and translate each into plain English.

days.title: The boast and the fight
days.work: Read the Unferth exchange and the fight with Grendel. Write a paragraph analyzing what Beowulf's boast reveals about the heroic code, citing two quotations.

days.title: Grendel's mother
days.work: Read the episode of Grendel's mother. Chart parallels and differences between the first two battles and discuss why the poet includes revenge as a motive.

days.title: Weekly check
days.work: Take a 20-question reading quiz on Beowulf so far and write a timed 20-minute response: 'Is Beowulf motivated more by glory or by duty?'

weeks.assessment: Reading quiz plus timed analytical paragraph scored for evidence.

objectives: Analyze the theme of mortality and legacy
Compare a modern retelling to the original

days.title: The dragon
days.work: Read the dragon episode and Beowulf's death. Annotate how the tone shifts from triumph to elegy.

days.title: Wiglaf and loyalty
days.work: Analyze Wiglaf's speech to the cowardly thanes; write a paragraph on how the poem defines loyalty and what happens when the comitatus fails.

days.title: Another perspective
days.work: Read the opening chapter of John Gardner's Grendel and compare how the monster is characterized. Complete a two-column comparison chart.

days.title: Grammar: appositives
days.work: Mini-lesson on appositive phrases (Beowulf's epithets are appositives). Write five sentences about the poem using appositives correctly punctuated.

days.title: Explanatory essay
days.work: Write a 600-word explanatory essay: how does Beowulf define a good leader, and what does the ending suggest about the limits of heroism?

weeks.assessment: Explanatory essay scored on thesis, evidence, and organization.

objectives: Analyze Chaucer's characterization and estates satire
materials: The Canterbury Tales (modern verse translation, Project Gutenberg or library)

days.title: Chaucer's England
days.work: Read about the three estates (clergy, nobility, commoners) and the Black Death. Listen to a recording of the opening 18 lines in Middle English and compare to a modern translation.

days.title: The pilgrims I
days.work: Read the General Prologue portraits of the Knight, Prioress, Monk, and Friar. Chart each character's ideal role vs. actual behavior.

days.title: The pilgrims II
days.work: Read portraits of the Wife of Bath, Parson, Miller, Summoner, and Pardoner. Mark lines of verbal irony where Chaucer's narrator praises a flaw.

days.title: Language change
days.work: Study how English changed from Old to Middle to Modern (vocabulary from French, loss of inflections). Translate four Middle English lines with a glossary.

days.title: Create a pilgrim
days.work: Write a 20-line modern 'General Prologue' portrait of a contemporary type (influencer, politician, coach) using Chaucer's ironic praise technique; take a vocabulary quiz.

weeks.assessment: Modern satirical portrait and vocabulary quiz.

weeks.topic: The Pardoner's Tale and the Wife of Bath
objectives: Analyze irony and moral in an exemplum
Compare medieval texts on a common theme
materials: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight excerpt (library)

days.title: The Pardoner's Tale
days.work: Read the Pardoner's Prologue and Tale. Identify the moral ('greed is the root of evil') and explain the double irony of who is telling it.

days.title: Wife of Bath's Tale
days.work: Read the Wife of Bath's Tale and answer: what does the knight learn women most desire, and how does the tale both challenge and reinforce medieval views of women?

days.title: Gawain's test
days.work: Read the beheading game and the girdle episode from Sir Gawain and the Green Knight; list how chivalric ideals are tested.

days.title: Grammar: pronoun clarity
days.work: Mini-lesson on vague and ambiguous pronoun references. Revise a paragraph about the Tales to eliminate every unclear 'it,' 'this,' and 'they.'

days.title: Unit 2 test
days.work: Take a unit test on Beowulf, Chaucer, and Gawain including a 40-minute comparative essay: how do two medieval texts test the ideals of their society?

weeks.topic: Macbeth Act I – prophecy and temptation
objectives: Analyze how Shakespeare establishes ambition and the supernatural

days.title: Shakespeare's stage
days.work: Read background on the Globe, James I, the Gunpowder Plot, and witchcraft beliefs. Learn to scan a line of iambic pentameter and mark stresses in three lines.

days.title: Act I, scenes 1–3
days.work: Read I.1–I.3 aloud with a parent taking parts. Analyze 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' as the play's motif of equivocation.

days.title: Act I, scenes 4–5
days.work: Read I.4–I.5. Paraphrase Lady Macbeth's 'unsex me here' soliloquy line by line and identify her strategy.

days.title: Act I, scenes 6–7
days.work: Read I.6–I.7. Annotate Macbeth's 'If it were done' soliloquy for imagery and reasoning; chart his arguments for and against the murder.

days.title: Act I check
days.work: Memorize and perform 10 lines from a soliloquy; take an Act I quiz on plot, character, and figurative language.

weeks.topic: Macbeth Acts II–III – murder and guilt
objectives: Track motifs of blood, sleep, and darkness

days.title: The dagger
days.work: Read II.1–II.2. Analyze the dagger soliloquy and the 'sleep no more' exchange; start a motif tracker for blood, sleep, and darkness.

days.title: The porter and discovery
days.work: Read II.3–II.4. Explain the comic relief of the Porter scene and how unnatural events in nature reflect the murder.

days.title: Banquo's fear
days.work: Read III.1–III.2. Compare Macbeth's reasoning for killing Banquo with his earlier hesitation about Duncan; write a paragraph citing two quotations.

days.title: The banquet
days.work: Read III.3–III.6. Watch the banquet scene in one filmed production and discuss how staging the ghost (visible or invisible) changes meaning.

days.title: Motif paragraph
days.work: Write a 400-word analytical paragraph tracing one motif through Acts I–III with at least four embedded quotations.

weeks.assessment: Motif analysis paragraph scored on evidence and commentary.

objectives: Analyze the resolution of the tragic arc

days.title: The apparitions
days.work: Read IV.1. Explain how each apparition equivocates and how Macbeth's misreading drives his overconfidence.

days.title: Macduff's grief
days.work: Read IV.2–IV.3. Compare Macduff's grief with Macbeth's response to loss; discuss what the play defines as true manhood.

days.title: Sleepwalking
days.work: Read V.1. Analyze Lady Macbeth's prose speech and how her guilt reverses Act II's 'a little water clears us of this deed.'

days.title: Tomorrow and tomorrow
days.work: Read V.2–V.8. Perform and analyze the 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow' soliloquy as Macbeth's final worldview.

days.title: Compare productions
days.work: Watch the same scene in two filmed versions and complete a comparison chart on setting, casting, cuts, and tone; discuss which is more faithful.

weeks.topic: Macbeth argument essay and the sonnets

days.title: Claim and counterclaim
days.work: Choose a prompt (e.g., 'Who is more responsible for Duncan's murder?') and draft a thesis plus a counterclaim you will rebut. Build an evidence outline.

days.title: Draft body
days.work: Draft the full argument essay (900–1,200 words) with embedded quotations and act/scene/line citations.

days.title: Sonnets
days.work: Read Sonnets 18, 73, and 130. Label the quatrains, volta, and couplet; explain how 130 parodies the Petrarchan blazon.

days.title: Revise essay
days.work: Revise the argument essay for transitions between claims and to strengthen the rebuttal paragraph; edit for verb tense consistency (literary present).

days.title: Unit 3 check
days.work: Submit final Macbeth essay and write a 14-line Shakespearean sonnet of your own in iambic pentameter.

weeks.assessment: Argument essay (W.11-12.1 rubric) and original sonnet.

materials: Pope, 'The Rape of the Lock' Canto 1 excerpt

days.title: Age of Reason
days.work: Read a short overview of the Enlightenment and the Irish famine context. Read 'A Modest Proposal' paragraphs 1–10 and mark the persona's calm, logical tone.

days.title: The proposal
days.work: Finish 'A Modest Proposal.' Chart each satirical technique (statistics, understatement, mock-logic) and identify Swift's real proposals in paragraph 29.

days.title: Mock epic
days.work: Read an excerpt from Pope's 'The Rape of the Lock' and explain how epic conventions applied to a trivial event create Horatian satire.

days.title: Modern satire
days.work: Analyze one modern satirical article or sketch: identify the target, technique, and real argument; compare with Swift.

days.title: Write satire
days.work: Write a 500-word 'modest proposal' on a current issue using a deadpan persona; include a hidden real solution.

weeks.assessment: Original satire scored on persona, technique, and clear target.

objectives: Identify Romantic ideals: nature, emotion, imagination, the individual
materials: Poems: Blake 'The Lamb' and 'The Tyger,' 'London'; Wordsworth 'Tintern Abbey' excerpt; Shelley 'Ozymandias'; Keats 'Ode on a Grecian Urn'

days.title: Blake's contraries
days.work: Read 'The Lamb,' 'The Tyger,' and 'London.' Compare innocence and experience and annotate how 'London' critiques industrial society.

days.title: Wordsworth
days.work: Read the preface definition of poetry as 'spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings' and lines from 'Tintern Abbey.' Write about a place that has changed for you.

days.title: Shelley and Keats
days.work: Read 'Ozymandias' and 'Ode on a Grecian Urn.' Discuss what each poem says about time, art, and permanence.

days.title: Explication method
days.work: Learn the explication method (literal, figurative, sound, structure, theme). Explicate 'Ozymandias' collaboratively, line by line.

days.title: Timed explication
days.work: Write a 40-minute timed explication of an unseen Romantic poem (e.g., Wordsworth's 'The World Is Too Much With Us').

weeks.assessment: Timed poetry explication scored on an AP-style 6-point rubric.

objectives: Connect the novel to Romantic and scientific contexts
materials: Mary Shelley, Frankenstein (1818 text, Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Origins
days.work: Read Shelley's 1831 introduction about the ghost-story contest at Lake Geneva. Read Walton's letters 1–4 and note how Walton mirrors Victor.

days.title: Victor's education
days.work: Read chapters 1–3. Track Victor's influences (Agrippa, Paracelsus, Waldman) and his attitude toward knowledge.

days.title: The creation
days.work: Read chapters 4–5. Annotate the creation scene for Gothic diction and analyze Victor's immediate reaction.

days.title: Vocabulary in context
days.work: Use context clues and Greek/Latin roots to define 15 words from chapters 1–5 (e.g., 'ardour,' 'countenance,' 'lassitude'); build a vocabulary log.

days.title: Reading check
days.work: Take a reading quiz and write a paragraph on why Shelley subtitled the novel 'The Modern Prometheus.'

objectives: Analyze the creature's narrative and education

days.title: Justine's trial
days.work: Read chapters 6–8. Discuss Victor's silence during Justine's trial and what it shows about his sense of responsibility.

days.title: Mont Blanc
days.work: Read chapters 9–10. Connect the sublime Alpine setting to Romantic poetry from Unit 4.

days.title: The creature speaks
days.work: Read chapters 11–13. List what the creature learns from the De Lacey family and from Paradise Lost, Plutarch, and Werther.

days.title: Rejection
days.work: Read chapters 14–17. Hold a seminar discussion: is the creature born good and made monstrous, or responsible for his own choices?

days.title: Seminar reflection
days.work: Write a 300-word post-seminar reflection citing one idea you heard and how it changed or confirmed your view.

weeks.assessment: Seminar participation rubric and written reflection.

objectives: Analyze doubling and the novel's resolution

days.title: The broken promise
days.work: Read chapters 18–20. Analyze Victor's reasons for destroying the female creature and the creature's threat 'I shall be with you on your wedding-night.'

days.title: Losses
days.work: Read chapters 21–23. Chart every death in the novel and who Victor blames for each.

days.title: Arctic ending
days.work: Read chapter 24 and Walton's final letters. Discuss why Walton turns back and how the creature's final speech reframes the novel.

days.title: Grammar: semicolons and colons
days.work: Mini-lesson on semicolons, colons, and dashes in Shelley's long sentences. Write six sentences about the novel using each correctly.

days.title: Theme chart
days.work: Build a theme map showing how two themes (e.g., responsibility and isolation) interact across the novel, with six quotations; take a final reading quiz.

objectives: Connect the novel to a modern issue
materials: one article on AI or bioethics (CommonLit or library)

days.title: Paired nonfiction
days.work: Read a contemporary article on AI or gene editing. List three ways it echoes Victor's choices.

days.title: Thesis & outline
days.work: Write a nuanced thesis on 'Who is the real monster?' or 'What does Frankenstein warn about creators?' and outline with evidence.

days.title: Draft
days.work: Draft a 1,200-word literary argument that includes one paragraph connecting the novel to the modern article.

days.title: Revise & edit
days.work: Revise using a parent's feedback; check MLA in-text citations and Works Cited for the novel and article.

days.title: Submit
days.work: Submit the final essay and complete a self-assessment against the argument rubric.

days.title: Timeline review
days.work: Build a literary timeline from Anglo-Saxon to Romantic periods, placing each text read with one defining trait of its period.

days.title: Archetype seminar
days.work: Discuss the 'overreacher' archetype across Beowulf, Macbeth, and Victor Frankenstein; take notes for the final.

days.title: Vocabulary & grammar review
days.work: Review the semester's vocabulary logs and grammar lessons with a practice test on appositives, pronouns, and punctuation.

days.title: Final exam
days.work: Take the semester final: multiple choice on passages, short answers, and a 45-minute synthesis essay comparing two works.

days.title: Portfolio reflection
days.work: Select your two best pieces of writing and write a 400-word reflection on how your writing changed this semester.

weeks.assessment: Semester final exam and portfolio reflection.

objectives: Analyze dramatic monologue and Victorian themes of doubt and duty
materials: Browning 'My Last Duchess'; Tennyson 'Ulysses'; Arnold 'Dover Beach'; Christina Rossetti 'Goblin Market' excerpt

days.title: Victorian age
days.work: Read an overview of industrialization, empire, and Darwin's impact on faith. Read 'Dover Beach' and annotate imagery of retreating faith.

days.title: My Last Duchess
days.work: Read Browning's 'My Last Duchess' aloud. Infer what happened to the Duchess and what the Duke unknowingly reveals about himself.

days.title: Ulysses
days.work: Read Tennyson's 'Ulysses' and compare its ideal of striving with Beowulf's heroism.

days.title: Write a monologue
days.work: Write a 30-line dramatic monologue in which a speaker reveals more than they intend to an implied listener.

days.title: Poetry quiz
days.work: Take a quiz identifying speaker, auditor, and irony in an unseen dramatic monologue; share your monologue aloud.

weeks.assessment: Original dramatic monologue and poetry quiz.

objectives: Analyze realist drama and social critique
materials: Henrik Ibsen, A Doll's House (Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Act I
days.work: Read Act I. List every pet name Torvald uses for Nora and what each suggests about their marriage.

days.title: Act II
days.work: Read Act II. Analyze the tarantella as a symbol of Nora's desperation.

days.title: Act III
days.work: Read Act III. Annotate Nora's final conversation for shifts in power and analyze the door slam.

days.title: Seminar
days.work: Hold a seminar: Is Nora's leaving heroic, selfish, or both? Support claims with lines from all three acts.

days.title: Response essay
days.work: Write a 600-word response tracing how Ibsen develops Nora's transformation across the three acts.

objectives: Analyze comic satire of Victorian manners
Compare two treatments of marriage and respectability
materials: Oscar Wilde, The Importance of Being Earnest (Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Act I
days.work: Read Act I. Collect five epigrams and explain the paradox in each (e.g., 'The truth is rarely pure and never simple').

days.title: Act II
days.work: Read Act II. Analyze 'Bunburying' as a satire of the double life demanded by Victorian respectability.

days.title: Act III
days.work: Read Act III. Discuss how the absurd ending mocks the obsession with names and social class.

days.title: Stage vs. screen
days.work: Watch one scene from a filmed production and evaluate how performance choices heighten the comedy.

days.title: Comparison essay
days.work: Write a 45-minute comparative essay on how Ibsen and Wilde use different modes (realism vs. comedy) to critique marriage and respectability.

weeks.topic: Empire: context and Things Fall Apart Part One
objectives: Analyze Okonkwo's character and Igbo society

days.title: The empire's voice
days.work: Read Kipling's 'The White Man's Burden' as a primary source. Analyze its rhetoric and assumptions about colonized peoples.

days.title: Chapters 1–5
days.work: Read chapters 1–5. Build a character profile of Okonkwo including his fear of being like his father, Unoka.

days.title: Chapters 6–9
days.work: Read chapters 6–9. Analyze the death of Ikemefuna and its effect on Okonkwo and Nwoye.

days.title: Proverbs
days.work: Collect 8 proverbs from Part One and explain how Achebe uses them to show the sophistication of Igbo oral culture.

days.title: Reading check
days.work: Take a reading quiz and write a paragraph on how Achebe's portrayal of Umuofia answers Kipling's poem.

weeks.topic: Things Fall Apart Parts Two and Three
objectives: Analyze the arrival of missionaries and colonial government

days.title: Exile in Mbanta
days.work: Read chapters 14–19. Discuss how exile and the missionaries' arrival change Okonkwo's status and family.

days.title: Nwoye's choice
days.work: Analyze why Nwoye converts, citing the hymn passage; compare father-son conflicts here and in Part One.

days.title: Part Three
days.work: Read chapters 20–25. Annotate the final paragraph and the Commissioner's planned book title.

days.title: The Second Coming

days.title: Debate

objectives: Write a literary argument using a critical lens
materials: Achebe, 'An Image of Africa' (library or anthology)
excerpt of Conrad's Heart of Darkness (Project Gutenberg)

days.title: Conrad excerpt
days.work: Read the opening river-journey passage of Heart of Darkness and note how Africans are described.

days.title: Achebe's critique
days.work: Read 'An Image of Africa' and outline its premises, evidence, and conclusion about Conrad.

days.title: Evaluate the reasoning
days.work: Write a one-page evaluation of Achebe's argument: which premises are strongest, and what counterarguments exist?

days.title: Essay draft
days.work: Draft an 800-word essay: How does Things Fall Apart function as an answer to colonial literature?

days.title: Revise & submit
days.work: Revise for precise claims and integrated quotations; submit with a one-sentence statement of your lens.

days.title: Choose a topic
days.work: Brainstorm five topics connected to a career interest or a literature theme; narrow one into an open, arguable research question.

days.title: Library databases
days.work: Use your public library's free databases (e.g., Gale, EBSCO) and Google Scholar to find six candidate sources; record full citation info.

days.title: Evaluate sources
days.work: Apply the CRAAP test (currency, relevance, authority, accuracy, purpose) to each source and keep the four strongest.

days.title: Proposal
days.work: Write a one-page research proposal: question, why it matters, working hypothesis, and planned sources.

days.title: Conference
days.work: Present the proposal in a 10-minute conference with a parent/mentor and revise the question based on feedback.

weeks.assessment: Approved research proposal and source evaluation chart.

objectives: Take accurate notes with paraphrase, summary, quotation

days.title: Paraphrase practice
days.work: Practice paraphrasing three passages without patchwriting; compare to originals and fix any borrowed phrasing.

days.title: Note cards
days.work: Read two sources and create 15 tagged notes (quotation, paraphrase, or summary) with page numbers.

days.title: More notes
days.work: Read two more sources and add 15 tagged notes; flag where sources agree or disagree.

days.title: MLA formatting
days.work: Learn MLA 9 container format; write Works Cited entries for a book, journal article, website, and interview.

days.title: Annotated bibliography
days.work: Submit an annotated bibliography of 6–8 sources, each with a 100-word summary and evaluation.

weeks.assessment: Annotated bibliography scored for accuracy and evaluation quality.

objectives: Organize evidence in a detailed outline

days.title: Synthesis matrix
days.work: Build a synthesis matrix mapping each subtopic to what each source says; identify a gap or debate.

days.title: Thesis
days.work: Draft three versions of a thesis and choose the most specific, arguable one.

days.title: Primary research
days.work: Conduct a short interview or survey (5+ responses) or analyze a primary document related to your question; record results.

days.title: Outline
days.work: Write a full sentence outline with topic sentences, evidence assignments, and a counterargument section.

days.title: Outline check
days.work: Submit outline; meet to confirm every section has at least two sources.

objectives: Draft an 8–10 page paper integrating sources

days.title: Introduction
days.work: Draft the introduction with a hook, context, and thesis; learn to use signal phrases ('According to…,' 'X argues…').

days.title: Body section 1
days.work: Draft the first major section (2–3 pages), pairing every quotation with at least two sentences of commentary.

days.title: Body section 2
days.work: Draft the second major section, including your primary research findings.

days.title: Counterargument
days.work: Draft the counterargument and rebuttal section, fairly representing the strongest opposing source.

days.title: Conclusion & check
days.work: Draft the conclusion (implications, not repetition) and submit the complete rough draft.

weeks.topic: Revising and editing the research paper

days.title: Reverse outline
days.work: Create a reverse outline of your draft (one sentence per paragraph) and reorder or cut paragraphs that don't advance the thesis.

days.title: Feedback
days.work: Get written feedback from a reader (parent, mentor, or tutor) using a research-paper rubric; prioritize three revisions.

days.title: Revise
days.work: Make the three priority revisions and strengthen transitions between sections.

days.title: Edit
days.work: Edit sentence by sentence for parallelism, hyphenation, and comma usage; run a plagiarism self-check against notes.

days.title: MLA polish
days.work: Format the paper in MLA (header, title, page numbers, hanging-indent Works Cited) and submit the revised draft.

objectives: Begin converting research to a presentation

days.title: Abstract
days.work: Write a 150-word abstract summarizing question, method, findings, and significance.

days.title: Final proofread
days.work: Do a final read-aloud proofread and submit the 8–10 page Senior Research Paper.

days.title: Present data
days.work: Turn one key finding into a clear chart or infographic with a source caption.

days.title: Storyboard
days.work: Storyboard a 10-minute presentation: hook, question, findings, counterargument, conclusion, Q&A.

days.title: Reflection
days.work: Write a research reflection: what surprised you, what you would do differently, and what question remains.

objectives: Analyze WWI poetry's rejection of heroic tradition
materials: Owen 'Dulce et Decorum Est'; Brooke 'The Soldier'; Sassoon 'Suicide in the Trenches'; Eliot 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock'

days.title: Before and after
days.work: Compare Rupert Brooke's 'The Soldier' with Wilfred Owen's 'Dulce et Decorum Est'; chart contrasts in imagery and attitude.

days.title: Sassoon and Owen
days.work: Read Sassoon's 'Suicide in the Trenches' and Owen's 'Anthem for Doomed Youth'; explain how the sonnet form is subverted.

days.title: Prufrock I
days.work: Read 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' aloud; annotate fragmented images and the speaker's paralysis.

days.title: Prufrock II
days.work: Discuss how Prufrock's allusions (Hamlet, Lazarus, Michelangelo) show alienation; compare to Victorian dramatic monologue.

days.title: Timed analysis
days.work: Write a 40-minute timed poetry analysis comparing Owen and Brooke on war and sacrifice.

objectives: Analyze absurdism and alienation in Kafka
Interpret symbolism in a Modernist novella

days.title: Part I
days.work: Read Part I. Discuss why Gregor worries more about his job than his transformation; mark deadpan narration.

days.title: Part II
days.work: Read Part II. Track how each family member's treatment of Gregor changes and what the apple symbolizes.

days.title: Part III
days.work: Read Part III. Analyze the ending's tone and the family's 'new dreams.'

days.title: Interpretations
days.work: Read two short critical interpretations (economic, family, existential) and decide which is most convincing with evidence.

days.title: Essay
days.work: Write a 700-word essay on how Kafka uses an absurd premise to explore a realistic theme.

objectives: Evaluate the structure of an argumentative essay
Apply Orwell's rules to your own writing
materials: Orwell, 'Politics and the English Language' and 'Shooting an Elephant' (library or anthology)

days.title: Shooting an Elephant
days.work: Read 'Shooting an Elephant' and analyze how Orwell's personal narrative indicts imperialism.

days.title: Politics and the English Language
days.work: Read the essay; outline its structure (problem, examples, causes, rules) and evaluate its effectiveness.

days.title: Newspeak
days.work: Read the Appendix on Newspeak from 1984; connect it to euphemisms found in modern news or advertising.

days.title: Apply the rules
days.work: Revise a paragraph from your research paper using Orwell's six rules; annotate each change.

days.title: Modernism test
days.work: Take a unit test on Modernist poetry, Kafka, and Orwell with passage analysis and short essays.

days.title: Build slides
days.work: Build 10–12 slides following the 'one idea per slide' rule with images, charts, and minimal text.

days.title: Script
days.work: Write speaker notes and practice transitions so the talk runs 10–12 minutes.

days.title: Record rehearsal
days.work: Record a full rehearsal and critique your pacing, filler words, and eye contact.

days.title: Q&A prep
days.work: List the 8 hardest questions an audience might ask and prepare evidence-based answers.

days.title: Dress rehearsal
days.work: Deliver a dress rehearsal to a family member and revise based on their feedback.

objectives: Present and defend research to an audience

days.title: Defense day
days.work: Present your research to a panel of at least two adults (family, co-op, or community mentor) and answer 5 minutes of questions.

days.title: Evaluate a speaker
days.work: Watch a TED talk or classmate presentation and write an evaluation of its reasoning, evidence, and rhetoric.

days.title: Panel feedback
days.work: Review panel scoring sheets and write a response to the toughest question you received.

days.title: Op-ed
days.work: Turn your research into a 650-word op-ed for a general audience and submit it to a local paper or blog.

days.title: Reflection
days.work: Write a reflection on the full research process from question to defense.

weeks.assessment: Defense scored by panel rubric; op-ed draft.

objectives: Reflect on growth as a reader and writer

days.title: Select work
days.work: Choose five pieces for your senior portfolio: a PIQ, a literary analysis, a timed write, the research paper, and a creative piece.

days.title: Revise one piece
days.work: Revise one earlier piece using everything you've learned this year and note changes.

days.work: Write a 'letter to my future self' narrative about the year's reading, using a quotation from a text that mattered to you.

days.title: Publish
days.work: Publish the portfolio as a Google Site or bound binder with a reflective introduction.

courses.title: Precalculus with Statistics
courses.description: A college-preparatory course that deepens function analysis (polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric), adds vectors, matrices, complex numbers in polar form, sequences, series, and conics, and closes with a substantial statistics strand: data analysis, regression, probability, and inference. Students use Desmos and CODAP throughout and finish with a limits preview and an original statistical investigation.

units.title: Functions and Their Transformations
units.big_idea: A small family of parent functions, transformed and combined, models a huge range of situations.

units.title: Polynomial and Rational Functions
units.big_idea: Factors determine zeros, and zeros and asymptotes determine the shape of a graph.

units.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
units.big_idea: Logarithms undo exponentials and let us solve for time in growth and decay.

units.title: Trigonometric Functions
units.big_idea: The unit circle turns angles into coordinates and creates functions that model anything periodic.

units.title: Analytic Trigonometry, Triangles, and Polar Form
units.big_idea: Identities and the Laws of Sines and Cosines extend trigonometry to any triangle and to the complex plane.

units.title: Vectors and Matrices
units.big_idea: Vectors capture magnitude and direction; matrices organize data and solve systems all at once.

units.title: Sequences, Series, and Conic Sections
units.big_idea: Patterns that repeat by addition or multiplication can be summed, and conics are defined by distance.

units.title: Data Analysis and Regression
units.big_idea: Distributions and models summarize variability, but correlation alone never proves cause.

units.title: Probability and Random Variables
units.big_idea: Probability quantifies uncertainty and expected value guides decisions.

units.title: Statistical Inference and Decisions
units.big_idea: Random samples and experiments let us draw conclusions about populations with known uncertainty.

units.title: Limits Preview and Statistics Capstone
units.big_idea: Average rates of change point toward calculus, and a full investigation pulls the year's statistics together.

courses.subject: SCI
courses.title: Earth & Space / Environmental Science
courses.description: A capstone lab science built on the NGSS high-school Earth and Space Science performance expectations plus the environmental (human-impact and engineering) expectations. Students move from the life of stars and the origin of the elements to plate tectonics, Earth's climate system, natural hazards and resources in California, ecosystems and biodiversity, pollution, climate change, and engineering for sustainability, ending with an independent local environmental investigation. Every week includes a hands-on investigation with household materials or real NASA/USGS/NOAA data.
courses.framework: California Next Generation Science Standards (HS Earth and Space Sciences, HS-LS2/LS4 human impacts, HS Engineering Design); 2016 California Science Framework; California Environmental Principles and Concepts

standards.HS-ESS1-1: Develop a model based on evidence to illustrate the life span of the Sun and the role of nuclear fusion in releasing energy that reaches Earth as radiation.
standards.HS-ESS1-2: Construct an explanation of the Big Bang theory based on astronomical evidence of light spectra, motion of distant galaxies, and composition of matter in the universe.
standards.HS-ESS1-3: Communicate scientific ideas about the way stars, over their life cycle, produce elements.
standards.HS-ESS1-4: Use mathematical or computational representations to predict the motion of orbiting objects in the solar system.
standards.HS-ESS1-5: Evaluate evidence of the past and current movements of continental and oceanic crust and the theory of plate tectonics to explain the ages of crustal rocks.
standards.HS-ESS1-6: Apply scientific reasoning and evidence from ancient Earth materials, meteorites, and other planetary surfaces to construct an account of Earth's formation and early history.
standards.HS-ESS2-1: Develop a model to illustrate how Earth's internal and surface processes operate at different spatial and temporal scales to form continental and ocean-floor features.
standards.HS-ESS2-2: Analyze geoscience data to make the claim that one change to Earth's surface can create feedbacks that cause changes to other Earth systems.
standards.HS-ESS2-3: Develop a model based on evidence of Earth's interior to describe the cycling of matter by thermal convection.
standards.HS-ESS2-4: Use a model to describe how variations in the flow of energy into and out of Earth's systems result in changes in climate.
standards.HS-ESS2-5: Plan and conduct an investigation of the properties of water and its effects on Earth materials and surface processes.
standards.HS-ESS2-6: Develop a quantitative model to describe the cycling of carbon among the hydrosphere, atmosphere, geosphere, and biosphere.
standards.HS-ESS2-7: Construct an argument based on evidence about the simultaneous coevolution of Earth's systems and life on Earth.
standards.HS-ESS3-1: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the availability of natural resources, occurrence of natural hazards, and changes in climate have influenced human activity.
standards.HS-ESS3-2: Evaluate competing design solutions for developing, managing, and utilizing energy and mineral resources based on cost-benefit ratios.
standards.HS-ESS3-3: Create a computational simulation to illustrate the relationships among management of natural resources, the sustainability of human populations, and biodiversity.
standards.HS-ESS3-4: Evaluate or refine a technological solution that reduces impacts of human activities on natural systems.
standards.HS-ESS3-5: Analyze geoscience data and the results from global climate models to make an evidence-based forecast of the current rate of global or regional climate change and associated future impacts to Earth systems.
standards.HS-ESS3-6: Use a computational representation to illustrate the relationships among Earth systems and how those relationships are being modified due to human activity.
standards.HS-LS2-6: Evaluate claims, evidence, and reasoning that complex ecosystem interactions maintain relatively consistent numbers and types of organisms in stable conditions, but changing conditions may result in a new ecosystem.
standards.HS-LS2-7: Design, evaluate, and refine a solution for reducing the impacts of human activities on the environment and biodiversity.
standards.HS-LS4-6: Create or revise a simulation to test a solution to mitigate adverse impacts of human activity on biodiversity.
standards.HS-ETS1-1: Analyze a major global challenge to specify qualitative and quantitative criteria and constraints for solutions that account for societal needs and wants.
standards.HS-ETS1-2: Design a solution to a complex real-world problem by breaking it down into smaller, more manageable problems that can be solved through engineering.
standards.HS-ETS1-3: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs, including cost, safety, reliability, aesthetics, and social, cultural, and environmental impacts.
standards.HS-ETS1-4: Use a computer simulation to model the impact of proposed solutions to a complex real-world problem with numerous criteria and constraints.

units.title: Stars and the Origin of the Universe
units.big_idea: Light from distant objects reveals how the universe began, how stars shine, and where the elements came from.

units.title: Earth's Formation and History
units.big_idea: Rocks, meteorites, and other planets record Earth's 4.6-billion-year story.

units.title: Earth's Dynamic Systems and Plate Tectonics
units.big_idea: Heat from Earth's interior and water at its surface continuously reshape the planet, and changes in one system cascade through others.

units.title: Weather, Climate, and the Coevolution of Earth and Life
units.big_idea: Earth's climate depends on energy balance and the carbon cycle, and life has changed Earth as Earth has changed life.

units.title: Natural Hazards and Resources in California
units.big_idea: Where people live and how they use energy and minerals are shaped by hazards and resources, and every resource choice has costs and benefits.

units.title: Ecosystems and Biodiversity
units.big_idea: Biodiversity supports ecosystem stability, and human resource use can protect or erode it.

units.title: Water, Air, and Pollution
units.big_idea: Pollutants move through connected Earth systems, and technology can reduce their impact.

units.title: Global Climate Change
units.big_idea: Data and models show that human activity is changing climate at an unprecedented rate, with regional impacts in California.

units.title: Engineering for Sustainability
units.big_idea: Engineering design breaks global challenges into solvable problems with criteria, constraints, and trade-offs.

units.title: Capstone: Local Environmental Investigation
units.big_idea: Scientists answer local questions with data and communicate findings to their community.

courses.title: American Government & Civics (S1) / Economics (S2)
courses.description: Semester 1 (Principles of American Democracy) examines the philosophical foundations of the Constitution, rights and responsibilities, the three branches, landmark Supreme Court cases, elections, federalism with a focus on California state and local government, the media, comparative systems, and a civic action project. Semester 2 (Economics) covers scarcity and economic systems, supply and demand, market structures, the role of government, labor markets, macroeconomic indicators, fiscal and monetary policy, and international trade. Primary sources (Federalist Papers, court opinions, ballot measures, Fed statements, BLS data) anchor every week.
courses.framework: California History–Social Science Content Standards, Grade 12 (Principles of American Democracy and Economics); 2016 California History–Social Science Framework. Government codes are prefixed GOV-12.x and economics codes ECON-12.x.

standards.GOV-12.1: Explain the fundamental principles and moral values of American democracy as expressed in the Constitution and other founding documents.
standards.GOV-12.1.1: Analyze the influence of ancient Greek, Roman, English, and leading European political thinkers (Locke, Montesquieu, etc.) on the development of American government.
standards.GOV-12.1.2: Discuss the character of American democracy and its promise and perils as articulated by Alexis de Tocqueville.
standards.GOV-12.1.4: Explain how the Constitution balances the classical republican concern for the public good with the classical liberal concern for individual rights, and how the Declaration and Constitution join liberal constitutionalism and democracy.
standards.GOV-12.1.5: Describe separated and shared powers, the role of organized interests (Federalist 10), checks and balances (Federalist 51), an independent judiciary (Federalist 78), enumerated powers, rule of law, federalism, and civilian control of the military.
standards.GOV-12.1.6: Understand that the Bill of Rights limits the powers of the federal government and state governments.
standards.GOV-12.2: Evaluate and take and defend positions on the scope and limits of rights and obligations as democratic citizens.
standards.GOV-12.2.1: Discuss the meaning and importance of each of the rights guaranteed under the Bill of Rights and how each is secured.
standards.GOV-12.2.2: Explain how economic rights are secured and their importance to the individual and society.
standards.GOV-12.2.4: Understand the obligations of civic-mindedness, including voting, jury duty, military service, and community service.
standards.GOV-12.2.5: Describe the reciprocity between rights and obligations; why enjoyment of one's rights entails respect for the rights of others.
standards.GOV-12.3: Evaluate and take and defend positions on what the fundamental values and principles of civil society are, their interdependence, and the meaning and importance of those values and principles for a free society.
standards.GOV-12.3.1: Explain how civil society provides opportunities for individuals to associate for social, cultural, religious, economic, and political purposes.
standards.GOV-12.3.2: Explain how civil society makes it possible for people, individually or in association with others, to bring their influence to bear on government.
standards.GOV-12.4: Analyze the unique roles and responsibilities of the three branches of government as established by the U.S. Constitution.
standards.GOV-12.4.1: Discuss Article I of the Constitution as it relates to the legislative branch, including eligibility, terms, election, and powers of Congress.
standards.GOV-12.4.2: Explain the process through which the Constitution can be amended.
standards.GOV-12.4.3: Identify their current representatives in the legislative branch of the national government.
standards.GOV-12.4.4: Discuss Article II of the Constitution as it relates to the executive branch, including eligibility, terms, election, and powers of the president.
standards.GOV-12.4.5: Discuss Article III of the Constitution as it relates to judicial power, including the length of terms of judges and the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
standards.GOV-12.4.6: Explain the processes of selection and confirmation of Supreme Court justices.
standards.GOV-12.5: Summarize landmark U.S. Supreme Court interpretations of the Constitution and its amendments.
standards.GOV-12.5.1: Understand the changing interpretations of the Bill of Rights over time, including interpretations of basic freedoms (religion, speech, press, petition, assembly) in court cases.
standards.GOV-12.5.2: Analyze judicial activism and judicial restraint and the effects of each policy over the decades.
standards.GOV-12.5.3: Evaluate the effects of the Court's interpretations of the Constitution in Marbury v. Madison, McCulloch v. Maryland, and United States v. Nixon, with emphasis on checks and balances.
standards.GOV-12.5.4: Explain the controversies that have resulted over changing interpretations of civil rights, including Plessy v. Ferguson, Brown v. Board of Education, Miranda v. Arizona, Regents of the University of California v. Bakke, and United States v. Virginia (VMI).
standards.GOV-12.6: Evaluate issues regarding campaigns for national, state, and local elective offices.
standards.GOV-12.6.1: Analyze the origin, development, and role of political parties.
standards.GOV-12.6.2: Discuss the history of the nomination process for presidential candidates and the increasing importance of primaries.
standards.GOV-12.6.3: Evaluate the roles of polls, campaign advertising, and controversies over campaign funding.
standards.GOV-12.6.4: Describe the means that citizens use to participate in the political process (voting, campaigning, lobbying, filing a legal challenge, demonstrating, petitioning, picketing, running for office).
standards.GOV-12.6.5: Discuss the features of direct democracy in numerous states (e.g., initiatives, referendums, recall).
standards.GOV-12.6.6: Analyze trends in voter turnout; causes and effects of reapportionment and redistricting, with special attention to spatial districting and the rights of minorities; and the function of the Electoral College.
standards.GOV-12.7: Analyze and compare the powers and procedures of the national, state, tribal, and local governments.
standards.GOV-12.7.1: Explain how conflicts between levels of government and branches of government are resolved.
standards.GOV-12.7.2: Identify the major responsibilities and sources of revenue for state and local governments.
standards.GOV-12.7.3: Discuss reserved powers and concurrent powers of state governments.
standards.GOV-12.7.4: Discuss the Ninth and Tenth Amendments and interpretations of the extent of the federal government's power.
standards.GOV-12.7.5: Explain how public policy is formed, including the setting of the public agenda and implementation of it through regulations and executive orders.
standards.GOV-12.7.6: Compare the processes of lawmaking at each of the three levels of government, including the role of lobbying and the media.

standards.GOV-12.7.8: Understand the scope of presidential power and decision making through examination of case studies.
standards.GOV-12.8: Evaluate and take and defend positions on the influence of the media on American political life.

standards.GOV-12.8.2: Describe the roles of broadcast, print, and electronic media, including the Internet, as means of communication in American politics.
standards.GOV-12.8.3: Explain how public officials use the media to communicate with the citizenry and to shape public opinion.
standards.GOV-12.9: Analyze the origins, characteristics, and development of different political systems across time, with emphasis on the quest for political democracy, its advances, and its obstacles.
standards.GOV-12.9.3: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of federal, confederal, and unitary systems of government.
standards.GOV-12.9.4: Describe for at least two countries the consequences of conditions that gave rise to tyrannies during certain periods.

units.title: Foundations of American Democracy
units.big_idea: The Constitution blends ancient, English, and Enlightenment ideas to limit power and protect liberty.

units.title: Rights, Responsibilities, and Civil Society

units.title: The Three Branches
units.big_idea: Separated and shared powers force the branches to cooperate and check one another.

units.title: The Supreme Court and Landmark Cases
units.big_idea: The Court's interpretations of the Constitution change over time and reshape American life.

units.big_idea: Scarcity forces choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost.

units.big_idea: Government corrects some market failures, but its actions also have costs.

units.big_idea: Wages reflect supply, demand, and productivity in a changing global labor market.

standards.VA:Cr1.2.HSIII: Choose from a range of materials and methods of traditional and contemporary artistic practices, following or breaking established conventions, to plan the making of multiple works of art and design based on a theme, idea, or concept.
standards.VA:Cr2.1.HSIII: Experiment, plan, and make multiple works of art and design that explore a personally meaningful theme, idea, or concept.
standards.VA:Cr2.2.HSIII: Demonstrate understanding of the importance of balancing freedom and responsibility in the use of images, materials, tools, and equipment in the creation and circulation of creative work.
standards.VA:Cr2.3.HSIII: Demonstrate in works of art or design how visual and material culture defines, shapes, enhances, inhibits, and/or empowers people's lives.
standards.VA:Cr3.1.HSIII: Reflect on, reengage, revise, and refine works of art or design considering relevant traditional and contemporary criteria as well as personal artistic vision.
standards.VA:Pr4.1.HSIII: Critique, justify, and present choices in the process of analyzing, selecting, curating, and presenting artwork for a specific exhibit or event.
standards.VA:Pr5.1.HSIII: Investigate, compare, and contrast methods for preserving and protecting art; prepare and present artwork, including digital documentation.
standards.VA:Pr6.1.HSIII: Curate a collection of objects, artifacts, or artwork to impact the viewer's understanding of social, cultural, and/or political experiences.
standards.VA:Re7.1.HSIII: Analyze how responses to art develop over time based on knowledge of and experience with art and life.
standards.VA:Re7.2.HSIII: Determine the commonalities within a group of artists or visual images attributed to a particular type of art, timeframe, or culture.
standards.VA:Re8.1.HSIII: Analyze differing interpretations of an artwork or collection of works in order to select and defend a plausible critical analysis.
standards.VA:Re9.1.HSIII: Construct evaluations of a work of art or collection of works based on differing sets of criteria.
standards.VA:Cn10.1.HSIII: Synthesize knowledge of social, cultural, historical, and personal life with art-making approaches to create meaningful works of art or design.
standards.VA:Cn11.1.HSIII: Appraise the impact of an artist or a group of artists on the beliefs, values, and behaviors of a society.
